summary: Rear light of the 1909 Bellevue Range in the Christina River at Wilmington, Delaware: a cast-iron skeletal tower, automated in 1934, deactivated in 2001 when a landfill hid its beacon.

access.note: Reached across the Cherry Island Landfill, where admittance is restricted and permission is required.

facts.agency: United States Coast Guard (per NRHP nomination)

events.note: War Department obtained the site for a jetty at the confluence of the Delaware and Christina rivers
Act of 20 June 1906 authorized the Bellevue Range lights
Cast-iron pyramidal skeletal rear light tower
Fourth-order eight-panel Fresnel lens shipped 10 January 1909
Lens first lighted 15 March 1909, with an incandescent oil vapor lamp
Christiana Light and Edgemoor Beacon discontinued; old Christiana lighthouse became the keeper's dwelling
September 1928 hurricane cut away the river bank at the station and damaged the dwelling
Listed among stations with the highest general efficiency in their districts for the year (keeper William H. Johnson)
Resident keepers withdrawn; modified for automatic operation
Dravo Contracting Co. permitted to use unoccupied dwellings during Edgemoor Dike work
Lighthouse Service abolished; duties to the Coast Guard
Cherry Island Landfill opened immediately north of the light
Optic obscured by the landfill; beacon obstructed; no longer an aid to navigation
Modern light tower on the unobstructed northeast side of Cherry Island

notes_for_editor: (1) The USLHS place record gives coordinates 40.2005, -75.863 (in Pennsylvania) and flags them suspect; the record's 39.7203, -75.5179 matches the Christina River site, so the USLHS position is not copied. (2) Height and focal height conflict: the NRHP gives 105 ft (32 m) base to ventilator ball; USLHS gives tower 93 ft and focal height 105 ft; the record's focal height of 28 m is not supported by either. Unresolved; the story uses only the NRHP figure. (3) Keeper end dates conflict: USLHS carries William H. Johnson to 1938; the NRHP says manned to 1934 and automated 1934. Both stay in the text. (4) William E. Spicer: the roster ends his stint in 1911; the 1930 Bulletin says his death in 1912 came in his 39th year of service. The sources do not say where he was in 1912. (5) First-assistant names and dates come from the USLHS roster (NARA registers via the Anderson inventory) and are not checked in primary registers. Only George H. Buchanan is named in the story. (6) The 1928 storm: the Fourth District note sits in the Bulletin article 'The September Hurricane' (vol. III, 1 October 1928). The note gives no day for the Bellevue damage, so the story does not date it. (7) Chronicling America searches for 'Bellevue Range' in Delaware papers 1908-1912 and 'Bellevue Range Rear' with 'lighthouse' 1909-1934 returned only advertisements (the word 'range' as a stove), and no news item about the light. (8) The local Lighthouse Board report corpus covers 1891-1901 only, and the Commissioner corpus 1915-1922; the 1909-1912 construction years rest on the NRHP nomination alone. (9) The Commissioner's 1919 list (scan p. 439) records a change of illuminant at this station; the new illuminant is not legible there, so the acetylene date rests on the NRHP. (10) The 2001 replacement tower is not dated separately in any source read; the record's 2000 'first lit' for Tower 2 (Rowlett) is not supported by the NRHP and is flagged here, not corrected. (11) No new photographs were found or proposed; the Wikipedia article was used only as a lead and is not cited. (12) Sources read are the NRHP nomination (PDF, pages cited by number), the Bulletins for 1928, 1930 and 1931, the 1918-1923 index, and the USLHS record and roster. FACT-CHECK 2026-10-22: (a) the Christiana 1835 sentence is on NRHP PDF p. 6 (Section 7), so source 2 is now labelled Section 7 and used for it; (b) the test pile is now placed after the 15 Oct 1907 engineer's report (PDF p. 10); (c) Linwood Spicer's service at Marcus Hook is stated as his keeper post at death, not as the order of his service, because the 1930 notice does not give an order; (d) the NRHP spells the company 'Pittsburg'; the story uses the modern 'Pittsburgh'; (e) the nomination's 'approximately 200 yards' quotation gets a metric equivalent (about 180 m) outside the quotation marks.
